versions.body:
# Secret Timing and Root Directory Proposal

This page preserves a proposal that bundled two API issues together. It never became a settled implementation guide, and remains here because someone did continue investigating along this line of reasoning during review. Looking back now, the two issues are similar only in that "both occur near the creation path", and their dependencies are unclear.

The initial idea was straightforward: as soon as the Secret creation call returned, treat the version as available for the next step; in the same round of work, include the application's nested directory in the Backend creation request. The former was intended to eliminate waiting, while the latter was intended to spare callers from needing separate entry points for different repository layouts. The draft did not distinguish between "the request has been accepted" and "the version can be read by downstream services". Nor did it explain where the directory value came from, or whether an empty value was equivalent to the repository root. These were the main reasons the proposal was later abandoned.

## The Retained Old Proposal

The old proposal described version timing as a short chain: create the Secret, obtain the returned object, and proceed with authorization and subsequent configuration. Here, the "return" was treated as a completion signal, rather than merely as an operation handle. The benefit was a short call path, with failures contained within a single command; the cost was that, for asynchronous operations, errors would be attributed to the authorization or configuration stage even though the process might actually have stopped earlier.

No dedicated waiting logic was proposed at the time. This was not because the absence of timing issues had been confirmed, but because of concern that adding polling at the command layer would turn failure information about the original Secret operation into a hard-to-explain waiting error. This rationale focused too much on interaction length and did not supply the missing assessment of version state, so it can no longer serve as a basis for implementation.

The other half of the old proposal held that the root directory did not need its own parameter contract: default repository layouts would continue through the original creation path, and passing the directory through would only be attempted when the caller already had a nested application directory. This "attempt" was not clearly defined. It could mean that the request contained a value, or merely that a local path was used during preparation; these two cases differ in how the codebase is located after creation.

The old draft also assumed that the two changes could be rolled back together: if either issue arose, simply restore the original creation call. This assumption was also too optimistic. Waiting for a Secret version and the repository directory field belong to different boundaries, with the former affecting when subsequent access begins and the latter affecting which application directory the creation request describes. Sharing a single rollback action would only make it unclear during investigation which change caused the difference.

## Nearby Code Observed at the Time

The investigation started at `src/functions/secrets.ts`. The file header imported `../utils`, `../operation-poller`, `../gcp/cloudfunctions` and `../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2`. Seeing these imports together led people to view the version issue as "polling infrastructure already exists, so it can simply be wired in later". But these imports alone cannot determine whether polling should cover Secret creation, authorization actions, or another asynchronous operation; the old proposal treated this gap as an implementation detail that could be omitted by default.

This entry-point record offered no equally direct clues for directory passthrough. Early discussions grouped it with Secret more to fit both into the same GA closeout than because they shared a function or returned object. This led to a somewhat unreliable division of work in the old proposal: conservatively minimize added waiting on the Secret side and added fields on the directory side. This trade-off of "change a little less on both sides" did not set out comparable failure scenarios.

The related entry points examined later were APH-207 and APH-224. The former only required recording what "Secret Version Sequencing" actually returned or threw through the public entry point; the latter required using the repository's own paths to check hits and misses. They separated the two issues, but this page did not reach a new unified conclusion on that basis. In particular, a single hit cannot show that all nested directories will be preserved correctly, and a single Secret return cannot show that use immediately afterward will necessarily be stable.

## Candidate Approaches During Review

There were three options for version timing at the time.

1. Keep the old draft: proceed directly to the subsequent Secret workflow once the creation call returns. The advantage is that the call surface remains unchanged; the disadvantage is the weakest failure attribution.
2. Wait only when the return indicates an asynchronous operation. The advantage is that waiting is limited to paths that need it; the disadvantage is that it first requires identifying which information in the returned object represents an operation that can be waited on, and what still needs to be checked after waiting ends.
3. Split creation and subsequent access into two user-visible steps. The advantage is a clear error location; the disadvantage is a longer command workflow, with callers also having to manage the state of both stages.

The old draft chose the first option and left the second for "adding later if problems arise". This ordering was unsound: the second option depends not on a new requirement that appears only after a problem occurs, but on completion semantics that should have been confirmed from the outset. The third option did not enter implementation discussions only because there was no desire at the time to broaden the command changes, not because it had been proven unworkable.

There were also three ways to handle the root directory: rely entirely on the repository's default directory; pass a nested directory through unchanged whenever the caller supplies one; or validate the directory before constructing the creation request. The old draft favored the second, but did not clearly distinguish between an empty directory, a relative directory, and the repository root. The first is sufficient for simple repositories, but loses the application location already known to the caller; the third makes it easier to report errors early, but adds path checks and compatibility branches.

One counterexample that was not addressed at the time is retained here: the repository contains an application subdirectory, but the caller does not explicitly provide a directory value. The old proposal would classify this as a default layout, and whether the actual creation target would still be correct was not recorded at the time. Another type of counterexample is a caller-supplied value that points to a non-application directory within the repository. The old proposal did not specify whether to reject it, fall back to the root directory, or continue with creation.

## An Incomplete Follow-up Review

When APH-224 was later moved into review, the recorded rationale was that the implementation had been completed on an existing branch, so it was moved directly to review. This shows that the directory-path work was no longer merely a long-term option in the proposal; but it does not show whether Secret timing was addressed at the same time, nor does it provide evidence that both were part of the same change. The old page had previously misrepresented "the implementation is near the creation path" as "both can be signed off together", a judgment that should be marked as outdated.

The follow-up review did not produce a new assertion to replace the old proposal. The existing records support only two things: the actual behavior of version operations needs to be recorded separately, and hits and misses from repository path checks need to be recorded separately. They cannot be combined into a single set of passing criteria, much less can the directory-side review status be used to vouch for the Secret side.

## Provisional Closeout Guidance

If this proposal is still used for verification, first split Secret and directory into two records. The Secret record should be limited to the span between the creation call returning, subsequent actions starting, and the point where a failure occurs; the directory record should retain both a request using the default directory and a request specifying a nested directory. If both records are insufficient, the old assumptions of "return means completion" or "pass it through whenever a value is present" should no longer be used.

The originally planned rollback approach should also be split. If version access is found to occur before creation has stabilized, roll back only the arrangement that proceeds directly to subsequent actions; if the creation target is found not to preserve the application directory, withdraw only the assumption that the directory can be defaulted. Do not change the behavior of one because of an anomaly in the other.

This page has not been updated to establish a new API decision. It preserves a combined proposal that was once convenient during a round of closeout work, but whose boundaries were not clear enough. If the background needs to be reconstructed later, start separately with the actual return records from APH-207 and the path-check records from APH-224.

# Recovery troubleshooting tree: no Backend

When recovering a deployment, first confirm whether you're seeing "no Backend selected" or whether the project actually has no available Backend. The old notes handled these two cases and a missing Compute account in the same path. That combined assessment remains below; once you find an actual Backend, don't use it to infer the account's status.

From the deployment entry point, refer back to `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. First record the project and location selected for this attempt, along with the Backend name entered. These values are more useful than the generic terminal messages when you re-enter the creation or selection flow.

- If the query returns a Backend, stop following the "no Backend" recovery path. Return to service account resolution for that Backend and confirm whether the runtime account has been obtained. Don't substitute the Cloud Build default identity just because the default Compute account is missing. The two types of identity were separate in the implementation at the time.
- If no Backend is returned, first return to the Backend creation flow, retaining the project, location, and repository selections. Don't grant Secret access or start a rollout before the Backend has been created; the resulting access grant would not establish which backend it was intended for.
- If the creation or query flow has established the Backend but the Compute account is still missing, retrieve the project number again and check whether the default Compute identity has appeared. The old approach treated this step as the criterion for completed creation. It can only indicate that recovery is not yet complete; it cannot prove that Backend creation failed.
- If the account still hasn't appeared, stop at the identity check and record the project number, location, Backend name, and raw failure output from this attempt. Don't borrow the Cloud Build identity as a temporary substitute or create another Backend with the same name.

The old sequence of "restore the Compute account first, then continue with all subsequent actions" is no longer accurate enough: if a Backend exists, first confirm the runtime account it actually uses; if no Backend exists, there is no target for the access grant. This page is retained because it can still help keep the two branches distinct, but it does not cover deleted backends, backends with the same name in different regions, or explicitly configured service accounts. If you encounter any of these cases, stop at the Backend query results and do not apply this page's recovery logic.

# Managed Secret Release Migration Workflow

For this round's GA closeout, record the managed Secret's ownership tag separately from the release action. The previous practice was to proceed with the release as soon as the Secret appeared usable; ownership information, the IAM update, and rollout were completed in the same operation, making it difficult to tell which stage had become stuck when something went wrong.

The post-migration sequence is provisionally three steps: first confirm that the item being handled is a managed Secret and record its ownership tag; then initiate the required access authorization; only then start rollout. Here, "last" refers to the operation order; it does not mean that permissions are immediately available after the IAM request returns. The initial version does not contain enough records to determine how the waiting window should be assessed.

Do not delete the old path yet. If the new sequence cannot confirm before rollout whether authorization has taken effect, retain the original release entry point and mark that operation as pending review. Do not conflate a missing tag and permission propagation as the same failure.

versions.body:
# Managed Secret Deployment Migration Workflow

The first version linked Secret ownership labels, authorization updates, and rollout into a single sequence. That made it easy to remember, but unsuitable for review. Later revisions showed that callers really need a separate record of each of the three stages: labels answer "who owns this managed Secret," IAM answers "has the access grant been submitted," and rollout answers "at which step does deployment start." These three answers should not be replaced by a single success or failure message.

## Procedure before and after migration

The old approach usually started with the deployment command. If the Secret already existed, it went straight into rollout; if something failed later, the record often said only "deployment did not continue." This obscured two things: whether the ownership labels had been established before starting, and whether time had been allowed between completion of the IAM write and permissions taking effect in the relevant services.

Use the following boundaries for the migration:

1. Before granting access, confirm that the object being handled is a managed Secret and save the ownership labels as seen at that point. The labels identify the object at this step; do not use them to infer that IAM has taken effect.
2. Grant access to the Secret. After submitting the grant, do not immediately use rollout startup as confirmation of authorization.
3. Wait for IAM to propagate, and separately record any status or failure stage available during the wait.
4. Start rollout only after this propagation check is complete. The deployment record should distinguish "rollout has not started" from "rollout has started but has not completed."

This does not require copying a large record for every deployment. For routine migrations, the labels, grant submission, and rollout starting point only need to be kept together in a record that can be consulted later; for migrations that encounter problems, also retain the failure stage and downloadable artifacts. This prevents an object selection error before authorization from being mistaken for a rollout issue during review.

## Retaining the old entry point

The old entry point can still serve as a recovery path, but label checks should no longer be skipped. During recovery, stop before rollout first: confirm that the Secret's ownership labels match the target of this deployment, then resubmit the access grant. If the propagation status of IAM still cannot be determined, do not start a new rollout. This restores the ability to operate through the old entry point, not the old "deploy first, explain later" sequence.

The first version's criterion, "seeing that the Secret is available is enough to continue deployment," no longer applies. Secret availability only means that the object itself can be found; it does not replace confirmation that authorization has propagated. This correction comes from work within the scope of this round of compatibility checks and should not be generalized to all Secret Manager scenarios.

## Review records

APH-209 is used to flesh out the observable differences for Managed Secret Ownership Label between successful and failed calls. The card was first included in deployment scope, and work on it began afterward; it is not, on its own, a basis for deciding whether rollout can start.

APH-226 records routine integration for starting rollout after IAM has propagated. Risk review and the subsequent start of work have already taken place, but the card actions themselves specify neither a propagation window nor the outcome of any particular rollout. This page therefore leaves "how to assess the wait" open, rather than inferring a specific duration or success criteria from the card's status.

## Where to look

The old navigation for Secrets points to `src/functions/secrets.ts`. Near this file, you can see `utils`, `operation-poller`, and imports for Cloud Functions v1 and v2. When investigating where a deployment stopped, you can start here to look for Secret operations and adjacent polling, but do not attribute all rollout orchestration to this file on that basis.

Another set of checks covering build identity and runtime identity is in DOC-22. It shares this page's deployment context, but does not replace the record here of ownership labels, IAM propagation, and rollout order.

# Managed Secret Release Migration Process

During the wrap-up of GA, issues with managed Secrets are particularly likely to be recorded as a single "release failure": some people see an incorrect label, some see that authorization has just been submitted, and others are already waiting for rollout. Once these fragments are put into the same result field, the next investigation has to start over by guessing how far the process had reached at the time. This record preserves the migration process, focusing on two related but distinct things: ownership labels for managed Secrets, and the sequence of starting rollout only after IAM propagation is complete.

The earliest release path had no explicit stopping points. After confirming that the Secret existed, operators would add authorization and continue the release in the same operation. This approach was short when everything went smoothly, but failures left behind a conflated set of symptoms: there was no way to tell whether the Secret being handled was the intended managed Secret, or whether rollout had started before authorization propagated or had become stuck after starting. The first version therefore proposed "three separate steps for labels, authorization, and release", but at the time there was still no way to assess propagation status.

Later work to organize routine integration did not fill this gap with a fixed wait time. Waiting for IAM propagation is not a timer-based action; what needs to be checked is the state after authorization is submitted, and whether rollout has not yet started. Without both of these, "we have already waited a while" cannot justify proceeding. The current migration guidance therefore retains an explicit stopping point: after updating authorization, check propagation first; if propagation cannot be assessed, stop before rollout.

## Misleading Assumptions Left by the Old Path

The following reflects the original intent of a side note in the first version, and is retained because some old operation records still use this interpretation:

> Once the Secret can be found, you can start the release first, then check authorization afterward based on the release result.

This passage has been deprecated. It compresses object existence, Secret ownership, writing IAM, and permission propagation into a single signal that it is "safe to proceed". During the actual migration, being able to find the Secret only means that object verification can begin, not that the selected Secret's ownership label has been confirmed, much less that the relevant access permissions have taken effect for the identity used by rollout.

Another old habit is to treat the ownership label as supplementary text in the release log. This loses its most useful function: identifying the managed Secret targeted by the current operation before authorization. The label is not used to assess IAM or determine rollout success; it simply allows subsequent records to distinguish object selection from permission propagation. The requirement to retain one label snapshot for a successful call and one for a failed call is still being tracked in APH-209.

## Sequence After Migration

The migration does not require reworking all Secret operations, only constraining this path involving managed Secrets and App Hosting releases. Follow this sequence:

**First, verify the object.** When you find the managed Secret to be handled, record its visible ownership label. The question to answer here is "which object does this authorization and release target". If the label is missing or cannot be matched to the release target, stop here; do not start rollout first to test whether the object is correct.

**Next, submit access authorization.** Record the authorization action separately as submitted. The record should not say "the release is ready" at this point, because completing the IAM write is not the same as completing permission propagation. If the authorization action itself fails, preserve the fact that the failure occurred at the authorization stage; do not classify it as a rollout failure.

**Wait and check propagation.** This stage does not end after a universally applicable number of seconds. Check whatever propagation status is available, or explicitly record that the status cannot yet be determined. Do not proceed to rollout without a propagation assessment. This stopping point may seem like an extra step compared with the old path, but it prevents authorization that has not yet propagated from being misrecorded as a release orchestration anomaly.

**Finally, start rollout.** Record the start of rollout as a separate event. This makes it possible to distinguish two kinds of failure: one where the process stopped before rollout, possibly because of object verification, authorization submission, or propagation status; and another where rollout has already started, requiring further investigation along the release and operation-polling path. Do not cover both cases with "deployment failed".

This path can be condensed into the following operational sketch:

```text
Old path
Secret exists ──> Submit authorization ──> Immediate rollout
                    │
                    └── All three stages mixed together on failure

Current path
Ownership label check ──> Submit IAM update ──> Propagation check ──> Start rollout
     │                    │               │
     └── Stop if object is unclear     └── Stop if submission fails └── Stop if status is unclear
```

"Stop" in the diagram does not declare the release permanently failed, but prohibits using the result of the next stage to explain the previous one. For example, if the label does not match, do not proceed with authorization; if authorization was not submitted successfully, do not start rollout; if propagation status is unclear, do not use rollout as a tool to detect whether propagation is complete.

## Recording Migration Batches

When migrating legacy callers for the first time, there is no need to reconstruct all historical release records. Simply start with the entry points that still handle managed Secrets and record the new sequence in the operation records. Retain at least four stage-specific details each time:

- Whether the Secret currently being handled has the expected ownership label;
- Whether the IAM update has been submitted, or at which stage submission failed;
- The status obtained from the propagation check, or why it cannot be determined yet;
- Whether rollout has not yet started, has already started, or at which stage it failed after starting.

These four points are not a checklist of pass criteria. They correspond to the points where the migration may branch. There is no need to continue collecting rollout logs for a call whose label is unclear; a call with an unknown propagation status also does not need to be treated as though it has entered the release stage. Conversely, records for a rollout that has already started should retain the locations of its subsequent artifacts, so the next investigation does not have to start over from Secret authorization.

The scope of APH-226 is to integrate "Start Rollout After IAM Propagation" into maintainers' day-to-day release workflow, and to record failure stages separately from downloadable artifacts. The card has undergone a risk review and work on it has started, but the existing records do not provide a fixed propagation time, specific commands, or a complete successful example. This page therefore does not prescribe how long to wait or interpret "downloadable artifacts" as any particular type of file; during migration, it only requires that they be recorded separately from the failure stage.

APH-209 retains the inventory of actual observations for Managed Secret Ownership Label: successful and failed calls should have their visible results recorded separately. Do not assume in advance that a failed call necessarily has no label, and do not infer from a successful call that all managed Secrets use the same label. Its purpose is to make object identification traceable, not to replace assessment of IAM or rollout.

## Returning to the Old Entry Point

The old entry point is still retained so that release operations can return to a usable starting point when the new sequence cannot be completed, not to restore the old decision-making approach. Recovery starts before rollout:

1. Return to Secret object verification and confirm that there is no mix-up involving the managed Secret for this operation and the ownership label records.
2. If the previous IAM update was not submitted or failed, handle the authorization stage again; do not directly label the original failure as a rollout failure.
3. If authorization has been submitted but propagation still cannot be confirmed, remain at the propagation check and do not bypass this stage by starting rollout early.
4. Restart rollout only after the propagation check is complete, and record this start separately from the previous record of a rollout that did not start or failed.

Recovery records should explicitly state whether "rollout never started" or "rollout started and needs to be retried". In the former case, there is no release orchestration result to interpret; only the latter requires preserving artifacts related to the release stage. Previously, conflating these two cases caused recovery actions to sometimes resubmit IAM and sometimes skip object verification.

If the label record is found to be inconsistent with the actual release target during migration, simply return to object selection and do not continue with IAM or rollout. If the label matches and authorization has been submitted, but propagation status cannot be confirmed, retain that status and wait for a later assessment; do not arbitrarily relabel it as "insufficient permissions" or "rollout service failure". These are different diagnostic directions.

## Relationship to Code Navigation

In the old troubleshooting notes, the issue names and call names point to `src/functions/secrets.ts`. The following direct dependencies are visible near that file:

```ts
import * as utils from "../utils";
import * as poller from "../operation-poller";
import * as gcfV1 from "../gcp/cloudfunctions";
import * as gcfV2 from "../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2";
```

This navigation is useful for starting from Secret operations and examining adjacent tool calls and operation polling. It should not be taken as a conclusion that "all release logic is here": this page is concerned with how the migration sequence is recorded in actual operations, not with assigning implementation ownership to that file. When investigating a rollout that has already started, continue from the code adjacent to `operation-poller` to find where polling actually occurs; if the issue is still at the label or IAM propagation stage, first return to the three prerequisite stages on this page rather than immediately broadening the search to release failures.

DOC-22 records another related check, namely Cloud Build Identity Differentiation and Backend Runtime Identity Passthrough. The two pages will be opened during preparation for the same release, but their recording purposes differ: this page does not use the other page's conclusions about identity as a substitute for Secret ownership labels, nor does it infer build or runtime identities from the propagation stopping point on this page. When both need investigation, first use this page to determine whether rollout is allowed to start, then go to DOC-22 to review the separate identity-side records.

## Operational Examples Still to Be Added

The current guidance has already established the sequence, but reusable examples from actual operations are still missing. The next time a successful call occurs, add the actual records spanning the ownership label, the IAM submission point, the propagation check, and the rollout start point; the next time a failed call occurs, first identify which stage it stopped at. In particular, cases where "authorization has been submitted but propagation cannot be assessed" must not be left with only a vague release failure label afterward.

The changes in this record are limited to this: labels identify objects, IAM propagation is a prerequisite check for rollout, and rollout itself is recorded separately once it starts. # App Hosting Identity Evolution Record

This record originally dealt with a naming confusion. Around Backend creation, both Developer Connect Proxy Domain and the default identities for Compute and Cloud Build were mentioned. It was not unusual to write them side by side in meetings: all were related to App Hosting work in the same project, and all appeared during troubleshooting in the form of an account or service name. The problem was that appearing side by side made it easy to read them as having the same source, and then as identities available at the same stage.

The initial draft took a straightforward approach: rather than defining a "project default account" that covered every case, it first retained, in the record, the service to which each name belonged. This decision did not resolve every anomaly involving permissions, creation, or runtime; it only prevented investigators from using one name to stand in for another. In retrospect, this scope is narrower than the wording of the initial draft suggested, but it remains the part of this old record worth retaining.

## Tradeoffs in the Initial Draft

At the time, there were three possible approaches.

| Approach | Benefit at the time | Reason for not adopting or retaining it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record the proxy domain, Compute, and Cloud Build uniformly as the project default identity | The notes in the creation path would be short | Names at the same level do not imply the same service source, and anomalies would lose their point of attribution. |
| Choose one preferred account only at Backend creation | It appeared to centralize the decision at the entry point | The creation entry point alone cannot explain what the later build and runtime each depend on. |
| Record clues separately by service name, then trace them back through adjacent implementations | The notes are more fragmented | Adopted. More fragmented, but it will not turn the proxy domain into an alias for the build or runtime account. |

The first approach later became the easiest to misuse. It treated "default" as a property that could propagate across services: once an account that looked reasonable was found, it was assumed to explain the other stages as well. The initial draft did not establish that such propagation was valid, so it did not include it in the decision. The second approach was also set aside. Backend creation is an entry point that needs attention, but the existence of that entry point cannot substitute for judging the boundaries of build and runtime.

The retained third approach is not a complete identity model. It is more like an order of operations: first confirm whether the subject is Developer Connect Proxy Domain, the Compute default identity, or the Cloud Build default identity; then decide which side's implementation or runtime records to inspect. The cost is that a single issue leaves several short notes, rather than one seemingly complete unified conclusion. The initial draft chose to accept this cost.

## Earlier Judgments and Their Problems

The initial draft described "the proxy domain has already appeared" as too close to an exclusion criterion, as if the default identity issue could be set aside for the time being as long as a name existed on the Developer Connect side. This sentence was not deleted because it explains why someone prioritized checking Developer Connect at the time; however, it is no longer suitable as a judgment of service readiness.

The proxy domain is an access clue for Developer Connect. The default identities for Compute and Cloud Build, by contrast, are names raised in different service contexts. They can both come up in the same Backend creation task, but they cannot be substituted for each other merely because they are in the same project. The initial draft's shared label made discussion easier, but its cost was that it brought "seeing a name" too close to "confirming that identity is used at a particular stage."

Another old practice should also be preserved in its original form: when an identity anomaly occurs, first look for an explicit value near the configuration, then use that value to explain creation, build, and runtime. This approach can occasionally narrow down the issue, but it overextended the local meaning of an explicit service account. The existing record does not support the claim that "an explicit value overrides all stages." The paragraph that previously treated it as a unified precedence is preserved as an old judgment and is no longer a basis for new review.

## Clues Left by the File Review

A later review returned to `src/gcp/devConnect.ts`. The file header directly imports `Client`, and also imports `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin`. These three names appear in the same local adjacency, which is why this record continues to retain the file as an entry point for verifying Developer Connect.

What is most useful here is not the filename itself, but that the two origin names were not folded into generalized default-identity naming. `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin` keep the Developer Connect side separately identifiable. The review therefore narrowed the initial draft's broader wording: the proxy domain is not another spelling of an arbitrary default account, nor should it be replaced by a project-level account conclusion.

This review did not interpret the import of `Client` as the entirety of the Backend creation responsibility, nor infer a call order from the two origin names. The file header can establish only that the current file is adjacent to the API client, the Developer Connect service entry, and its P4SA entry. For a history record, this is enough to correct the name categorization; it is not enough to write all creation, build, and runtime relationships as an established implementation.

To prevent the old notes from merging the three categories of clues again, the state sketch from that time was retained. It describes branching at registration, not a service call graph.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Name source pending verification" as Pending
    state "Developer Connect Proxy Domain" as DevConnect
    state "Compute default identity" as Compute
    state "Cloud Build default identity" as CloudBuild

    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> DevConnect : Proxy domain
    Pending --> Compute : Default identity
    Pending --> CloudBuild : Default identity
```

The three endpoints in the diagram do not indicate execution order, nor that any two of them can be interchanged. It merely draws the recording action decided on in the initial draft: when the same "default identity" wording appears, it cannot stop at the shared label; it must first resolve to the side to which the relevant name belongs.

## Revised Decision

The decision retained on this page is now stated in four points.

First, Developer Connect Proxy Domain is recorded separately as a Developer Connect clue. It can direct verification to `src/gcp/devConnect.ts`, but cannot replace confirmation of the Compute or Cloud Build default identity.

Second, the Compute and Cloud Build default identities are recorded separately. Both contain the word "default," but that does not provide a basis for equating them. The presence, absence, or explicit configuration of one side cannot directly establish the status of the other.

Third, the Backend creation record is responsible only for describing the names and choices observed at creation; it does not make inferences about the build and runtime stages. When a particular stage needs further discussion, write the stage name and service name together rather than adding a vague "default account confirmed."

Fourth, file review prioritizes locally visible object names. For Developer Connect topics, `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin` are more suitable starting points for tracing back than generic account terms. If a new implementation location later uses these names, add an explanation at that location rather than expanding this page into a summary of all identity paths.

These four points revise the initial draft's wording, but they do not overturn its core tradeoff: names from different services cannot be combined into a project-level fact merely because they belong to the same App Hosting project. The quick judgments in the old text can still help readers understand why name sources were checked first at the time; they just can no longer be treated as directly actionable identity-determination rules.

## Still-Retained Outdated Parts

This record still uses "Compute and Cloud Build Default Identity Separation" as the discussion topic. That topic is useful for reminding readers not to merge the two clues, but it does not provide complete identity rules for every service in every situation. Early material presented it as a way of handling things that could cover creation, build, and runtime; that was an overextension and no longer applies.

Likewise stale is the troubleshooting sequence of "find the easiest-to-see account first." It may produce a candidate value when configuration is missing, but a candidate value is not a conclusion. If the name comes from Developer Connect, it only indicates that the Developer Connect side is worth examining further; if the name is referred to as the Compute or Cloud Build default identity, it can only first be returned to its respective service context and should not be casually assigned to the other line.

This page was not reorganized into a current configuration guide. It preserves the evolution of the decision during the closeout of GA: first using a shared label to facilitate discussion, then discovering that the shared label obscured the source, and therefore changing the recording method to separate entries by service line. For anyone still citing the old notes, this is more useful than leaving only a final one-sentence conclusion, because it shows which statements came from early convenience and which were narrowed after the file review.

## Boundary with Adjacent Topics

Backend Default Repository Path Creation and Secret Authorization Region Selection are adjacent topics here, but are not decided by this page. They may likewise involve service names or accounts, but each has its own creation parameters and authorization choices. Mixing these topics into the identity history would recreate the substitution relationship the initial draft tried to avoid.

This page leaves only one reusable decision method: when an adjacent topic includes a name from Developer Connect, Compute, or Cloud Build, first identify which service line the name belongs to; only if that topic itself requires it should you continue asking about its relationship to Backend creation, build, or runtime. This prevents a local entry point from being expanded into a project-wide identity conclusion.

What remains unresolved is the scope to which an explicit service account applies across different stages. The existing file review did not answer this question, so "explicit account takes precedence" was not written into the decision. If material about a specific stage is added later, first state what it covers, then decide whether the boundary retained here needs to be changed.

# Same-name Backend Region Troubleshooting Tree

When multiple Backends with the same name appear during a release, do not select an object by name alone. The name only narrows the candidates; the region is the second condition for this investigation. Record the Backend name provided by the caller, the target region, and the final returned status together before moving on to code review.

## Split into two cases first

**Region provided**

1. Reproduce candidate filtering with the name and region together.
2. If only one candidate remains, continue verifying that the object received by the caller is that candidate; do not skip the return-value check just because the names match.
3. If more than one candidate remains, stop automatic selection. Record the region of each candidate and return to the caller side for input that can distinguish the objects.

**No region provided**

1. First confirm that same-name candidates actually exist in the environment, rather than that old output was mixed into the list result.
2. When multiple candidates exist, do not treat the first result in the list as the answer. Have the caller specify the target region, then retry.
3. Even with only one candidate, retain the scope of this list result; if another region is added later, the same name may no longer be unique.

## Code review

The current navigation entry is `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. When reviewing it, follow the Backend filtering logic downward, focusing on how `region` participates in filtering and which branches contain `matches`, `list`, `message`, and the returned `object`, respectively. The goal here is to identify the branches for "no match," "unique match," and "duplicate name," not to infer ownership of a deployment command's implementation from the filename.

The top of the file also imports `../../gcp/cloudfunctions`, `../../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2`, `../../utils`, and `./runtimes/supported`. When candidates come from different generations of functions, record their sources separately first; do not merge same-name results from two entry points into one Backend.

## Stop conditions

If any of the following cannot be confirmed, do not continue making the region selection for the release:

- The caller has not provided the target region;
- There are more than two same-name candidates in the list;
- The returned object cannot be matched to a recorded candidate;
- The branch being reviewed does not show whether `message` handles no match or multiple matches.

The investigation record must include at least the name, region, candidate count, and actual returned status. This makes it possible to determine, the next time a same-name object appears, whether the input is missing a region or the filtering branch itself does not include the region in the match.

# Build and Runtime Account Grouping Proposal

GA During the closeout phase, start with a simple assumption: builds and runtime for the same Backend use the same group of accounts, with only one selection in the configuration flow. This avoids having to explain the differences between the build and runtime sides separately during creation, and Secret authorization can reuse the same selection.

There are two candidate approaches.

- Merged grouping: Select one group of accounts when creating the Backend, and take the values for both build and runtime from that selection.
- Separate grouping: Record the build account and runtime account separately during creation, then expand the authorization steps by purpose.

The initial draft leans toward merged grouping. This is not because the two types of tasks are considered identical, but because the most likely problem during closeout is that users know only the Backend name and not which side needs additional configuration. Splitting the selection into two parts would make the interaction, configuration, and troubleshooting entry points longer; merging them first keeps the issue scoped to the Backend level.

The trade-off is clear: once the build and runtime accounts actually have different permissions, the merged name will hide that distinction. The current draft still assumes this difference will occur only in a small number of special projects, with exceptions added when they arise rather than changing the default flow to use two groups.

The recommendation is to use the same grouping result at the creation and Secret setup entry points first. If a Backend later turns out to require separate account specifications, revert this merge: retain the Backend identifier, add separate build-side and runtime-side fields, and populate both existing configurations with the original selection. It has not yet been decided whether the exception should be exposed during creation or whether users should be asked to fill it in only after authorization fails.

# Build and Runtime Account Grouping Proposal

The initial draft treated "only one account group is needed for the same Backend" as the default consolidation approach. That judgment remains here: at the time, it addressed the problem of too many entry points, rather than establishing the responsibilities of the accounts. During a later review, the file originally treated as the wiring point provided narrower clues than expected; the draft was not rewritten into a two-account proposal on that basis, so both the old choice and its blind spots have been retained.

## Choices Left by the Initial Draft

The original plan was to put build and runtime accounts in the same group. When creating a Backend, the operator would make only one account selection; Secret settings would reuse the same result. The benefits were a shorter workflow and the ability to use the Backend name as the sole lookup target. The initial draft was especially concerned about another situation: users already knew which Backend they wanted to change, but were required to first distinguish whether the configuration issue was "on the build side or the runtime side." Merging the groups deferred that distinction so configuration could proceed to completion first.

The other option listed at the time was to separate them from the first step. The build account would be recorded separately, the runtime account would be recorded separately, and any step that depended on an account would read it according to its purpose. The advantage was straightforward field meanings; the disadvantage was having to explain where the two selections came from during initial configuration, and having to decide which side an existing set of values should go to when migrating old configurations. The initial draft did not design migration rules, and simply assumed that most Backends did not need this distinction.

That assumption is the draft's central risk. It treated "there should be fewer configuration entry points" as sufficient justification for "accounts can be shared." Without counterexamples, this inference looks convenient; with counterexamples, the proposal itself has no place to represent them, leaving callers to add ad hoc checks.

## Scope Observed During Review

This review started by looking back at `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. The file header directly imports `../../gcp/cloudfunctions`, `../../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2`, `../../utils`, and `Runtime` exported by `./runtimes/supported`. These adjacent dependencies show that the file touches both function deployment and runtime types; it does not provide a field table that can be used directly to group App Hosting build and runtime accounts.

The initial draft treated this path as the center of the grouping wiring because both issue names and call names had pointed here. After review, the only thing that can be confirmed is that it is a suitable place to continue looking for adjacent deployment-side code; these imports do not establish that account selection has already been completed here. In particular, the presence of `Runtime` shows, at most, that runtime types are locally visible; it does not indicate that runtime and build accounts should be shared, nor that the two have already been separated.

The toolchain-pinning action in APH-217 allows this review to continue on the same toolchain, but the card itself does not supply the source of the account fields. Thus, two premises of the old proposal remain unverified: whether the Backend already stores both types of accounts, and whether the result obtained from Secret settings can distinguish build use from runtime use.

## Wiring Still Proposed Under the Old Approach

The draft provisionally uses the Backend as the grouping key, rather than placing accounts directly in project-level defaults. Each creation or modification first locates the target Backend, then retrieves that Backend's account-group result. This at least prevents different Backends from overwriting one another through project-level defaults, and matches the initial draft's interaction assumption that "the user knows the Backend name first."

In this model, the build workflow reads the grouping result and then starts the build; runtime configuration uses the same result. Secret-related entry points also grant authorization only to this set of results. The grouping object's name can remain neutral, without being labeled "build account" or "runtime account" in the configuration interface, because the initial draft's premise is precisely that the two sides are not separated for now.

The proposed workflow does not require turning `backend.ts` into the sole entry point. That file is the starting point for this review, and both function deployment and runtime dependencies can be traced further from here; where account selection takes place still needs to be confirmed along the call relationships. To keep the workflow name from obscuring this gap, the draft recommends retaining only two checks before wiring: whether the target has been resolved to a specific Backend, and whether the retrieved account result is empty. It does not define which type of default identity should be selected automatically when the result is empty.

If later implementation finds that the same Backend already has two distinguishable account sources, the old proposal would still favor collapsing them into one group. This is not because having two sources is meaningless, but because the initial draft gave compatibility with old configurations more weight than accurately expressing purpose. After collapsing them, callers would not need to add two sets of parameters immediately either; the cost is that, during troubleshooting, the group name cannot indicate whether a failure belongs to build or runtime.

## Trade-offs Accepted at the Time

Merging the groups would broaden the scope of authorization. The initial draft accepted this, considering configuration omissions, rather than confusion over permissions, to be the main source of failures during consolidation. It therefore put "being able to complete a Backend configuration" ahead of "explaining each account by purpose." This ordering was not validated against actual permission differences, and no exception list was developed for different Backends.

Separating the groups would instead trade the risk for migration costs. If an existing Backend has only one account value, splitting it requires choosing whether to copy it into both fields, write it only to the build side, or write it only to the runtime side. All three migrations could change existing behavior; the initial draft did not want to introduce this choice while consolidating GA, so it did not adopt the separation approach.

There was also a third compromise: keep one account group on the surface, store separate build and runtime slots internally, and fall back to the shared value only when a slot is missing. This would leave an interface for future separation, but would leave invisible precedence rules even after configuration was complete. The initial draft considered this implicit fallback harder to troubleshoot than an explicit single-group rule, so it did not list it as the default approach.

## Conditions for Withdrawal

If investigation finds that build and runtime retrieve accounts from different sources, and one side cannot safely reuse the other side's account, the merged grouping should be withdrawn. When withdrawing it, the Backend should not be removed as the lookup key; only the results within the group should be split into build and runtime values, with new configurations required to fill them in explicitly. Old configurations should retain the shared value initially, with the decision about which side to write it to, or whether to copy it to both sides, deferred until migration.

If the problem is only that a particular call entry point does not pass the Backend down, that does not establish a need for two groups. For that type of problem, restoring Backend lookup is enough as a first step. Conversely, if the account result is empty, that empty value cannot be interpreted directly as a reason to merge; it may come from the selection chain, missing configuration, or failure to locate the correct Backend yet.

The most troublesome issue after withdrawal would be Secret authorization. The initial draft assumed that it could reuse the shared result; after separation, it must be made explicit whether authorization is for the build account, the runtime account, or both. There is no usable migration conclusion here, so the shared value cannot be expanded automatically into two authorizations without first confirming their purposes.

## Questions Still Unresolved

- After `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`, the actual call site through which account selection enters has still not been recorded in this draft.
- There is no conclusion yet on whether `Runtime` and account selection are on the same configuration chain.
- After the toolchain is pinned in APH-217, the specific configuration file in which missing build configuration items should be placed still needs to be checked separately.
- If separation is required, the draft has not decided whether the shared account value of an old Backend should be copied, migrated, or require a new selection.

What is retained here is therefore an old proposal that prioritizes reducing entry points, not a final account of account responsibilities.

# Caller Entry Point Trace-Back Workflow

This page preserves an old handoff path. The "current" in the entry-point filename refers to the revision being examined at the time of writing, and should not be taken to mean the project's only entry point today: `docs/adj-commands/notes/from-current-entry-to-current-revision.md` can still help people find the original material, but it has not been reorganized to reflect subsequent integration changes.

The original notes had only two reference points: `IAM propagation`, and `apphosting.yaml` immediately after it. At the time, the plan was to trace directly to `Firebase CLI`, because that name was also nearby; only on reviewing it later did it become clear that a call edge was missing in between. The old draft placed all three in a single line, which could easily give the impression that they already formed a sequence of entry point, configuration, and execution. What was actually preserved was only their proximity within the same replay.

## Start with the Original Sample

The constraint in APHA-005 is very narrow: use the original commands-client-integration for the replay, and do not reconstruct a similar input. The distinction here is that the caller integration test records preserve the objects from the actual sample and the order in which they appeared. Rerunning with another extension, another integration, or even parameters with the same names produces a new context and cannot replace the result first observed on the old page.

After opening the entry page, first find the caller object to which the replay is attached, then check whether `IAM propagation` appears before or after the input. The notes do not provide a complete internal chain to expand on, so this section has just one purpose: to identify whether this is a marker left on the propagation side or a marker on the configuration side. If the page treats it only as a side note, just copy down the object adjacent to that note; do not extend it into a complete permissions flow.

Next, look at `apphosting.yaml`. Here, it is not a declaration that "all callers must go through this", just the name of a project configuration file visible in the old sample. Its value is in helping you return to the original context: when a configuration file appears again in the replay, you can check whether it still falls within the same caller record. It does not resolve who called whom, nor can it explain on its own which layer the error exits from.

The old draft's TODO said "check whether the error is passed out unchanged or has its type changed in the layer above". No conclusion has ever been added for this question. When you encounter an error, first preserve its original text on the original entry page, then find the first point where it changes form; if the page does not preserve the outputs from both sides, write only "undetermined". Inserting a backend or rollout name encountered later back into this section does not make the type change verifiable.

## Two Places Where Names Should Not Be Conflated

`Firebase CLI` is the name in these notes most likely to be misread. It appeared, but was never linked back to a direct caller. The old version's statement that it "appeared nearby once" still holds; what no longer applies is the interpretation that it belongs to the entry layer. When tracing back through this old page now, seeing it should prompt you to return to the previous entry with an actual object relationship, rather than continuing to jump ahead based on names alone.

`Cloud Build Repositories` and `Developer Connect` present the same kind of problem. They were recorded as names alongside the material, and the old page did not provide enough connections to determine how the two affect caller integration. The purpose of keeping these two names is to let people return to the entry page and verify the context at the time, not to assemble them into a migration path. If a replay encounters only one of them, record that name and the adjacent object; do not fill in the missing steps for the other side.

Likewise, `location` can serve as a point to inspect during a location selection. It only indicates that the reader has reached the location-related section, and does not automatically imply that the backend that follows has been selected. Earlier notes treated "seeing location" as a signal to continue tracing the backend, but this shortcut no longer applies: without connected objects in the original sample, stop at location selection.

## Recovery Records Beside the Old Page

APHA-007 requires the recovery results to be placed alongside the original context. Two types of material are placed side by side here: the inputs and objects seen in the original failure window, and the recovery results appended afterward. Do not replace the failure window on the entry page with the post-recovery results, or later readers will see only a successful replay and be unable to tell whether it is still following the same path.

That is also why this page does not present "recovery" as a new starting point. Recovery results should be attached beside the original entry point, first checking whether they still correspond to the same commands-client-integration sample; if the object has changed, record it separately as a new context. The wording on the old page is fairly rough and can only provide the first branch point and the address to refer back to, not cover all integration differences.

A record related to an expiration action was once brought into this area, but it has since been marked as posted to the wrong card and does not belong to the same context as "placing the recovery results alongside the original context". It should not be used to explain the cause of the stall, nor should it be used to establish a chronological order for `IAM propagation` or `apphosting.yaml`. Keeping this correction prevents people from later reconstructing a nonexistent call chain backward from card titles.

## Where to Stop Reading

The first reliable place to stop on this old path is still at `IAM propagation` and `apphosting.yaml` in the original sample. If the adjacent objects between the two are still present, you can continue checking whether the configuration side belongs to the same replay; if only isolated names remain, do not pretend they are already connected.

The second stopping point is `location`. When it appears, check whether the page still retains the context of the same location selection; if there is no context, just record the name. The third stopping point is `Firebase CLI`: a direct caller is still missing here, and the old notes have no answer.

backend, rollout, `Secret Manager`, and service identity were mentioned across a broader set of materials, but they are not confirmed next hops on this page. They may be used as search terms, but must not be written up as subsequent steps from this entry point. This distinction may seem conservative, but it preserves the most useful part of the old page: it lets people return from an actual call sample to the first branch point, rather than moving from a string of familiar terms to an imagined chain.

Finally, two items remain unresolved:

- which direct caller `Firebase CLI` entered this replay through;
- whether the original error changed type in the layer above.

If either item is added to the entry page later, append the new observation beside the original object, and do not reorder the old paragraphs. The "current revision" in the old paragraphs is now a historical reference, but the original failure window and the original sample are still worth preserving.

# Caller Integration Testing: Two-State Postmortem

This anomaly showed up in caller integration test samples for integration and extension. The same object in the original record showed different current revisions when viewed at two different times through the current entry point. At first, this was treated as a mismatch between Secret Manager and the old record; location was later found to be recoverable, but the reason for the backend change remained unresolved.

The main impact was on integration assessments: recovery for the same call sample could no longer be judged solely by the final value on the page, nor could a single green result override adaptation boundaries or integration feedback. The object has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit actions, so speculation about adjacent paths was not treated as part of the cause.

First preserve the entry-point version used at the time and the original input; the entry point was `docs/adj-commands/incidents/commands-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. Stop retrying here: the recovery of location only shows that this one path is back; it does not explain why backend differs between the earlier and later records.

Confirmed so far, in chronological order:

- At the first comparison, the current entry point differed from the old record.
- The original state was preserved, not replaced with the page after recovery.
- After location recovered, the caller path was usable again.
- The backend change remains unexplained.

There are still gaps in the timeline. The available material is insufficient to attribute the difference between the two states to rollout, service identity, or adjacent services; none of these are included in this version's conclusions.
