versions.body:
# Dual-State Postmortem for Caller Integration Testing

This record preserves observations of the same object presenting two different states at different points during caller integration testing. It is not a summary that attributes all integration issues to a single cause. The object comes from real call samples involving integration and extension; it carries both adaptation boundaries and integration feedback. The page initially recorded a mismatch between the old record and the current entry point. Later, the page partially recovered, but that recovery did not erase the earlier record.

The easiest misreading of these observations is to take "it looks normal now" as "there was no difference earlier." When the entry point was first checked, the current revision in the record differed from the current revision seen on the subsequent check. Both referred to the same object, but the value ultimately displayed on the page only described the state at the time of viewing and could not replace the original record. The original input, entry-point version, and recovery page were therefore preserved; further retries stopped after location was confirmed to have recovered.

This is not a fault report covering all commands. The impact is limited to assessments based on this set of call samples: the integrating party obtained states for the same object that could not be directly pieced together, and the original adaptation conclusions could not be confirmed solely from the later page. The object has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit action. This postmortem does not list changes in other projects, states of other services, or paths that were not reproduced as its causes.

## Brief Notes Left at the Time

The initial brief notes contained only a few points: the observations in Secret Manager differed from the old record; location could later be restored; why backend had changed was still unknown. Those notes did not contain a complete set of timestamps, nor did they conflate recovery actions with root-cause confirmation. Their value was not in providing an explanation, but in preserving the fact that "different states had indeed been observed before recovery."

No nonexistent details were filled in at the time. In particular, a single page discrepancy was not presented as proof that the backend had rewritten the object, and the recovery of location was not extended into a claim that all integration-testing paths had recovered. Subsequent review followed the same constraint: first distinguish the state already observed, the state observed again after recovery, and the parts of the difference between them that remained unexplained.

"Secret Manager differs from the old record" in the original notes was wording used at the time, not a final attribution of cause. It described an inconsistency found during comparison and did not prove that Secret Manager itself caused the two states. The later write-up retained this sentence to show where the initial investigation began, not to elevate it into a conclusion.

## Sequence of Events

There are no reliable, precise timestamps to enter in this postmortem, so the events are listed in order of occurrence without presenting sequence as duration.

| Sequence | Observations | Action Taken at the Time | What Still Cannot Be Determined from This |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial comparison | The current entry point differed from the old record | Saved the original input and entry-point version | Which component caused the difference |
| Object checked again | The same object returned different current revision values at two viewing points | Kept both records without overwriting the earlier one with the later one | Whether there were undocumented intermediate changes between the two states |
| Scope narrowed | backend provided no answer that could explain the difference | Listed it separately as an unknown | Whether backend was the source of the change |
| Recovery observed | location could be restored | Recorded the recovery point separately from the discovery of the anomaly | Whether recovery explained the earlier revision difference |
| Retries stopped | The caller path recovered to a state that allowed integration to continue | Stopped attempts that would only repeat page observations | Whether the root cause had been confirmed |
| Follow-up organization | The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause still existed separately | Kept all three material locations | Rewriting the entire event using a single page value |

This sequence table deliberately does not invent "which minute," "which request," or any response value that was not retained. The available material supports only the order of events: the inconsistency was observed first, and location was observed to recover later; the reason for the backend change remains unknown. Keeping these relationships separate prevents the later appearance of the recovery page from being used to deny the initial observations retroactively.

## What Each of the Two States Means

The first state came from comparing the old record with the current entry point. It was an actual observation in an integration-testing sample, not a design assumption. It temporarily removed a single authoritative basis for the original integration assessment: the caller could not know whether to rely on the current revision in the old record or the current revision subsequently displayed at the entry point.

The second state came from a check after recovery. The recovery of location was a valid change, showing that at least this observed path was available again. But it answered only "has location recovered," not "why did backend change," nor did it establish which of the two revision values represented the state of the entire object across all adjacent paths.

There is therefore no contradiction in the event containing both "recovered" and "cause unknown." The former is an observation about a specific path; the latter is a causal assessment of the difference between the two states. Previously, placing these two statements too close together could lead readers to mistake recovery itself for the cause. The revised organization separates them: the recovery page records visible recovery; the unknown item records the gap in explanation.

Another easy source of confusion is the distinction between the object and the page. The page is what the current entry point displayed at a particular viewing point, while the old record preserves earlier observations. Both concern the object, but they are not interchangeable materials. The final page value can serve as supporting evidence, but it cannot erase the original observations. Keeping both is not intended to create a contradiction, but to ensure that subsequent reviews can still see that the difference once existed.

## State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldRecord: Preserve the old record
    OldRecord --> DivergenceSeen: Current entry point differs
    DivergenceSeen --> LocationRecovered: location recovered
    DivergenceSeen --> BackendUnknown: Reason for backend change unclear
    LocationRecovered --> EvidenceKept: Preserve the recovery page
    BackendUnknown --> EvidenceKept: Preserve unconfirmed items
    EvidenceKept --> [*]
```

The two branches in the diagram are not two separate incidents. They come from the same round of integration testing for the same object, separately representing the recovery already observed and the change that remains unexplained. Placing backend on the "cause unclear" side avoids a common but invalid leap: assuming that it caused the revision difference simply because it appears in the record.

Likewise, placing location on the "recovered" side does not mean that it must previously have failed at a particular layer. The available material shows only that it could be restored. Call details that were not preserved should not be filled in as a failure sequence involving an interface, configuration, permissions, or service internals.

## Why the Original Observations Were Not Cleared Away

The page after recovery is usually easier to reopen and more likely to become the only material cited. If it were the only thing retained, later readers would see an available path but would not see why the caller had stopped proceeding with integration based on the old record. The original observations are preserved here because the two states themselves are central to this anomaly, not to retain a screenshot of a page that has already been superseded.

The original input preserves the context when the difference occurred; the entry-point version preserves the state read at the time; the recovery page preserves the fact that location became available later. The three answer different questions: the first shows where the issue was discovered, the entry-point version shows what was displayed at the time, and the recovery page shows which path recovered. They do not replace one another.

Early notes tried to compress these materials into a single statement: "it has recovered now." That wording was quick enough for a temporary handoff, but could not support the next comparison: readers would not know whether different revision values had actually existed before recovery, or why the backend change remained listed as an unknown. Version 2 no longer uses this condensed assessment.

Preserving the original record also prevents the later stable state from being retroactively applied to the initial adaptation feedback. The caller's cautious assessment during the anomaly concerned the entry point seen at that time and should not be described as a false alarm merely because location later recovered. These are simply records from different state points.

## Scope and Impact

The affected materials are the real call samples involving integration and extension and their integration feedback. The samples are used to understand adaptation boundaries, so inconsistent states directly affect whether the integrating party can continue assessing the object's state based on the current entry point. The impact does not automatically extend to all App Hosting behavior or to callers that did not appear in the observations.

"Impact" here does not refer to an unrecorded production consequence. What is known is that the basis for assessment during integration testing became inconsistent: the old record and the later current entry point could not simply be treated as the same result. For maintenance actions, this means keeping the materials from before and after recovery side by side, rather than deleting the old items first and then declaring things normal.

The separate schedule, maintainer, and exit action are also part of the scope. This object should not be replaced by a broad status statement in the daily report, nor should changes underway in adjacent projects be listed as causes of this event merely because those projects are making other changes. This postmortem retains only the state differences and integration feedback that actually occurred for this object.

The original responsible person still needs to review the exit action before it is due; if there are no new observations, the existing exit action can be closed out based on the existing record. This action addresses only the materials left by these two states. It does not disguise an unknown root cause as resolved or create new conclusions for adjacent objects.

## Assessment Approaches That Did Not Hold Up

One initially convenient reading was to classify the event as a temporary display issue, since the recovery page already showed location as available. That reading was later withdrawn. It did not explain why the old record and the current entry point gave different current revision values, nor why backend remained an unknown. The fact of recovery can be retained, but it cannot be used to skip determining the cause.

Another reading centered on backend. Because it continued to be mentioned during the comparison, it was easy to attribute the change directly to backend. This assessment also lacked sufficient material. The record did not preserve any fact that directly linked backend to the revision difference; writing it up as the root cause would disguise an open question as a confirmed fact.

Another approach was to use only the final value from the later page. This could reduce conflicts in the document, but would lose the most useful part of the incident: why the caller could not continue using the old integration assessment at the earlier point. Version 2 explicitly does not use this cleanup approach. Only by keeping the original record, recovery page, and unknown cause together can readers reconstruct the decision boundaries at the time.

These abandoned assessment approaches are not irrelevant investigative tangents. They explain why brief notes are insufficient as long-term documentation: brief notes can tell the person taking over that the path has recovered, but cannot explain how the two states were discovered, which explanations did not hold up, or which questions remain unanswered.

## Changes in Understanding After Review

The subsequent review did not identify an additional component to hold responsible, but it changed how the event was organized. The materials were originally arranged around "whether the current page is normal," then reorganized around "anomaly discovery, recovery observation, cause unknown." The former arrangement lets the later state overwrite the earlier one; the latter allows the same object to leave different states at different viewing points without requiring one of them to be eliminated first.

What the review confirmed was not a complete technical chain, but the boundaries of this record: the object does belong to the independent incident track for commands-client-integration; the daily report should retain only a link, rather than compressing the two states here into a single project-status statement. The reason is practical: caller integration testing has its own real samples, adaptation boundaries, integration feedback, maintainer, and exit criteria.

"Current revision" is not a static label here. It is the value returned by the entry point at a particular viewing point. Different values at two viewing points constitute the anomaly that needs to be retained in this case. If a new value is seen in the future, the new observations and their relationship to the original record should be recorded separately, rather than directly modifying the two observations already preserved on this page.

The review also confirmed a stopping condition: unless new observations can link the difference to a specific change, no further answers will be sought by repeatedly checking the recovery page. Repeated checks can confirm the current display, but cannot automatically supply the reason it differed earlier. Stopping does not declare that the problem does not exist; it avoids fabricating new evidence from more observations of the same kind.

## Questions Still Open

There is still no conclusion as to why backend appears in the earlier and later records as an issue that needs to be listed separately. The available material does not establish whether it was the source of the state change, a side observation, or coexisting information with no direct relationship to the recovery of location. This question should remain as it is, rather than being overwritten by "the current path is available."

The available material also cannot answer whether there were undocumented intermediate states between the two current revision values. The postmortem confirms only that the two viewing points differed; without intermediate material, no continuous change curve should be filled in, much less an assumption that one of the readings was simply incorrect.

The recovery page can show that location has recovered, but cannot show that all adaptation boundaries have been revalidated. No extension or integration branch that did not appear in this event is declared to have passed here. If new real call samples become available later, they should be compared side by side with the earlier observations preserved on this page, rather than substituting old conclusions for new observations.

Finally, the missing precise timestamps remain missing. The sequence is sufficient to support this postmortem: the difference was discovered first, location recovered later, the reason for the backend change remained unclear, and repeated retries then stopped. There is no material supporting any other durations, frequencies, or intermediate actions. Leaving them blank remains more faithful to the observations than filling them into a precise narrative.

## Retention Location

The maintenance entry point remains `docs/adj-commands/incidents/commands-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. # Alternative Plan for Caller Integration Testing

The discussion at the time wasn't about reworking the entire integration surface, but about separating out the callers of commands-client-integration from the existing entry point. The two options on the table were straightforward: continue managing the call relationships through `apphosting.yaml`, or handle `Firebase CLI` as a separate integration segment. The latter looked like a direction worth trying at the time, but it wasn't a decision yet.

Keeping the existing entry point would avoid having to split up the existing configuration first, with fewer changes visible to callers. The problem was that the entry point's two failure exits didn't lead to the same place: one looked like processing hadn't continued on the configuration side, while the other looked more like the CLI side hadn't handled it. Treating both as the same kind of failure and adding another branch would probably only make diagnosis take longer. That assessment came from a draft found at the time, not from completed integration testing.

The idea behind splitting out CLI was to have callers first take a path that could be observed independently, while keeping the original entry point for comparison. It didn't require removing `apphosting.yaml` immediately, and the configuration file shouldn't be treated as the source of the error. During the trial, check only two things: whether callers actually enter the split-out path; and whether, on failure, it's possible to tell if they're still in the old entry point or have already entered the CLI segment. If neither is clear, this route should not be rolled out as the default integration path.

At the time, someone favored shutting off the old entry point outright. I didn't agree. Not because the old entry point was already reliable, but because we hadn't yet identified the callers using `Developer Connect`. Cutting off the entry point first would conflate "no calls" with "callers haven't caught up," making it hard afterward to tell whether the split itself was the problem or something had been missed in the integration surface.

The tentative rollback conditions were therefore fairly conservative: if the split-out path couldn't make the failure exits distinguishable, or if any unlisted callers were found to depend on the old entry point, restore only the old entry point, without also changing the configuration's meaning or writing up the trial as a rule already in effect. After restoring it, keep the comparison records from that time so the next attempt doesn't start by guessing from the same ambiguous entry point again.

Still undecided:

- Which active callers `Developer Connect` actually has;
- Whether rollback should only restore the old entry point or roll back the CLI segment as well;
- Which caller to start the trial with so that local observations aren't mistaken for broadly applicable results.

This proposal has no start date and doesn't name anyone to carry it out. The earlier draft is in `docs/adj-commands/proposals/not-adopted-commands-caller-integration-approach.md`; to revisit the material on the existing entry point, refer to DOC-30. This document preserves the route that wasn't adopted at the time and the rollback boundaries; later integration results should not be written back as conclusions that had already been confirmed then.

# Stalled quality signal troubleshooting tree

When firebase-vscode-quality-signal appears stalled at this entry point, first preserve the earliest failing sample. Do not start with a retry, or clear existing output just to trigger it again. On this signal dashboard, later output from the same test run may simply be fallout from an earlier failure; preserving the first anomaly is necessary to distinguish regression-layering issues from unstable signals.

The entry-point file is at `docs/adj-firebase-vscode/runbooks/firebase-vscode-quality-signal-when-stuck-who-to-escalate-to.md`. First find the record containing `operation poller` here, and collect the visible output, test log, or trace excerpts in the same place. Record only what has actually appeared; if there is no trace, do not fill in a runtime stage based on the description.

## First branch: Has it reached rollout?

**You have not seen `rollout`**

Stop at this entry point. At this point, all you can confirm is that the signal has not progressed to rollout. Do not attribute the issue to the backend or send it straight to the permissions maintainer. Preserve:

- the first failing sample, not a sample from a retry;
- the complete output segment from this test;
- any visible environment differences, such as whether the same signal also stalls in another environment;
- the step reached as shown at this entry point.

If a new trace becomes available, reassess from this branch. If there is no new material, stop troubleshooting and take no recovery action.

**You have seen `rollout`**

Leave the failure state intact. Continue by checking whether `service identity` has appeared. The point here is not to confirm that rollout was printed, but to check whether a service identity record was left after it. On one earlier occasion, an immediate retry after rollout overwrote the original failing sample with the later output, making it impossible to tell afterward whether polling had stalled or identity information had not been returned. This kind of retry is no longer used as the first step.

## Second branch: Has service identity appeared?

**Has not appeared**

Stop here. Record "rollout has appeared, service identity has not appeared" and send it to the permissions maintenance intake along with the first failing sample and environment differences. Do not fill in a service account yourself based on the missing information, or write this up as a confirmed permissions failure. If the maintenance intake needs new evidence, append only the output or traces it explicitly requests; preserve the existing sample unchanged.

**Has appeared**

Do not close the signal just because identity is present. Return to the original stalled behavior: if the test has resumed, record that recovery occurred after identity appeared; if the test is still stalled, the issue remains in firebase-vscode-quality-signal. Include the output boundaries before and after identity in the handoff. Do not repeat the earlier recovery actions in this branch.

## Recording environment differences

Record only environment differences you have actually observed through comparison. For example, if one sample has rollout and another stalls before the operation poller, preserve them separately rather than combining them into "the same failure." If there is no comparable sample, write "not compared"; do not substitute the result from this environment for a conclusion about another environment.

If the first failing sample has already been overwritten, first save whatever output is still available, then note that the original sample is missing; do not work backward from a later success or failure to infer where it originally stalled. Recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment. Unless there is already an explicit record from the same failure context, do not treat a local rerun as confirmation of recovery.

## Exit conditions

You can stop this round of troubleshooting when any one of the following applies:

- rollout has not appeared, and there is no new trace;
- rollout has appeared but service identity is missing, and the failure state has been preserved and handed off to the permissions maintenance intake;
- service identity has appeared but the test is still stalled, and the output boundaries before and after it have been recorded;
- the first failing sample cannot be recovered, so only the existing material can be saved and the gap noted.

Do not skip past the first point where evidence is missing to name a final cause. Open separate records for neighboring quality signals; do not combine them into a single conclusion in this tree.

The issue was again the same release object showing different current revisions at two entry points. Don't reduce it to "the page briefly failed to refresh": the build queue, artifact versions, and withdrawal window all changed around the records for `.github/workflows`. For at least part of that time, readers would infer two opposing current states from those records.

The incident was recorded in the following order. At T+00, `deploy-release automation-two states for the same object` was first observed to deviate from the baseline; the original input and entry-point version were saved. At T+07, `backend` was found to still be working normally, so the scope of impact was initially narrowed to downstream display or orchestration. At T+31, the user path recovered, but the root cause was not confirmed at the time of recovery.

```text
Consumer -> Release object entry point -> backend -> rollout
                       |
                       +-> Current revision in the old record
```

The initial working assessment was that, since `backend` was working normally, the queue itself was unlikely to have contributed to the discrepancy, and recovery could initially be explained as IAM propagation. The page timeline later failed to provide enough support for this assessment, but it was not removed at the time. # Release Automation Dual-State Postmortem

This record has not been removed from the knowledge base because the difference in state between two entry points once affected withdrawal decisions. Its early conclusions should no longer be treated as an investigation sequence, but the original incident evidence, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause have not been merged: the three describe different things at different times.

## The initial assessment

The first record described the issue as "Developer Connect differs from the old record". At the time, there was no complete request context and no run id that could map the queue, artifacts, and pages to one another individually. Because `backend` looked normal, the investigation at the scene was limited to the downstream side; because the user path eventually recovered, the record also stated "possibly IAM propagation".

This account remains here not because it is reliable, but because it did guide the on-call team's decision to stop: continued retries produced no new discrepancies, the original input was saved, and retries were stopped. Even then, recovery and cause needed to be recorded separately; the problem of mistaking recovery for the cause only became clear later.

Original entry point: `docs/adj-deploy/incidents/deploy-release-automation-same-object-has-two-states.md`. This involved the build queue generated by `.github/workflows`, artifact versions, and the withdrawal window. They belong to the same release automation object, but there is no guarantee that the "current" values on the same page came from the same read.

## Incident timeline

| Relative time | Preserved observation | Action at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `deploy-release automation-two states for the same object` first deviated from the baseline; the two entry points reported different current revisions | Saved the original input and entry-point versions, without replacing them with later pages |
| T+07 | `backend` was still normal | First narrowed the scope of impact, without directly identifying the queue as the point of failure |
| T+18 | Comparison information pointed to `rollout` | Handed subsequent checks over to the corresponding maintenance path |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Ended ongoing retries and left the root cause open |

The diagram at the time was drawn like this:

```text
Consumer
  |
  v
Release object entry point ----> Current revision in the old record
  |
  v
backend ----> rollout
```

The diagram only shows the reading order. It did not prove that the arrows represented calls, nor did it prove that `rollout` was the source of the anomaly. The early version worded "the comparison points to rollout" almost as an attribution of cause, which overstated the evidence; what was actually preserved was one comparison result and one handoff, not a root-cause report.

## Why "two states" affect withdrawal

The withdrawal window depends on the artifact version that is read. When both entry points are treated as current, the on-call team cannot decide which artifact to retain based on just one of them, nor can a green page at one entry point be taken to mean that the other has synchronized. The build queue came from `.github/workflows`, but no complete identifiers were preserved at the time to match every queue item to its page revision; the record therefore only preserved "two states for the same object", rather than turning the gap into a definite queue failure.

The initial approach was to save both pages, stop further retries, and wait for the user path to recover. This avoided backfilling the incident evidence with later final values, but left a practical question: after recovery, could the old entry point still be treated as the current entry point. Materials added after the second version showed that screenshots could not answer this question.

## Later challenges to the old assessment

In APHC-004, the maintenance record required marking when the current entry point changed and not directly subtracting the statistics for the two versions before and after the change. A related addendum said that execution records could be reconstructed, but the explanatory section for the current result came from an old mirror; the old mirror was later given a version label, and the provenance chain for the execution records was displayed separately.

This did not prove that the old mirror created the two states. It invalidated a narrower assumption: the first version treated the "current revision" read from each entry point as like-for-like data that could be compared directly. If the explanatory text came from an old mirror while the execution records came from a different preservation chain, the two might not belong to the same point in time even if they used the same object name.

APHC-010 subsequently required reordering the current revision and release automation records by their original times, with the final page values used only as corroborating evidence. "Corroborating evidence" has a specific meaning here: the final page can show that a particular value existed later, but it cannot replace the two states already saved at T+00, nor can it replace the missing time of the change. The early version did not make this distinction, so it could misread "consistent later" as "never diverged earlier".

After the old index was cleared in APHC-007, the execution records could still be opened from the history. This observation also undermined the claim that "the old entry point is no longer valid, so there is no need to check it". Whether the old index still exists is not the same as whether the history is readable; clearing an index and deleting incident evidence are two different actions.

## Incorrect attribution still retained

The following is the old account, retained for review and not as a basis for subsequent handling:

> `backend` was normal, which shows that the release automation chain had no problems; recovery of the user path shows that IAM propagation was complete, so the two states were just a display delay.

This statement once made it easier for the on-call team to wrap up, but it linked together three unverified leaps in reasoning. `backend` being normal only showed that this checkpoint displayed no anomaly; recovery of the user path only showed that recovery had occurred; there was no material at the time confirming whether the page discrepancy was a display delay. The later additions about the old mirror and page timing issues made "just a display delay" even less suitable as the default explanation.

However, the opposite conclusion—that all discrepancies were mirror problems—should not be asserted either. The available materials do not provide the entry-point write order or an item-by-item mapping between queue items and artifact versions, nor do they record the complete request process. The certainty of the old account can be rejected, but that does not justify filling in a new, definite root cause.

## Separating the records

The original record preserves the first discrepancy, the `backend` state seen by the on-call team, and the decision to stop retries. The recovery page preserves the outcome that the user path recovered. The unconfirmed cause is kept separately to prevent it from being silently changed into a conclusion after a page update.

This separation was the only aspect that stabilized during the incident. It also explains why the knowledge base contains seemingly duplicate materials for the same object: one answers "what was observed at the time", one answers "whether it recovered later", and another acknowledges that "why this happened is still unknown". They cannot overwrite one another.

## Items left unfinished at the time

- The timing and sequence of the first divergence between the two entry points have still not been filled in.
- No preserved record has been found that maps `.github/workflows` queue items, artifact versions, and page revisions to one another individually.
- There is still no usable explanation for the changes to `apphosting.yaml` in the old record; the early version placed it in the same paragraph as IAM propagation, but this was only co-occurrence, not causation.
- After `rollout` was handed off as a lead for comparison, no root-cause response was recorded here.

Therefore, the historical assessment preserved on this page is: after the anomaly occurred, the user path recovered at T+31; IAM propagation was used as a tentative explanation early on. A more reliable order for subsequent reading is to first compare the preserved points in time, then separately review the old mirror notes, execution records, and final page. Do not overwrite the incident evidence from T+00 with the final page's revision, and do not substitute `backend` being normal for checking the build queue, artifact versions, and withdrawal window.

Related navigation is retained as APHC-004, APHC-007, APHC-010; the operational checklist for exiting the window is at DOC-40.

# Release Automation Alternative

Deployment automation currently has two comparable paths: continue using `service identity`, or split `Web App` out of the existing path. The latter is retained here as a trial proposal, not treated as an implementation that has already been put in place as a replacement.

The split is not proposed simply to put the two terms in different queues. Existing records show that when the two paths each encounter a failure, they use different rollback exits. If they continue to share one processing chain, failures in the build queue will be attributed to the same entry point, and artifact versions and rollback windows will be difficult to assess separately. This difference is the basis for the current preference to split them; it is not enough to show that either side is already more stable.

During the trial, retain the original `service identity` entry point and open a separate `Web App` branch. The branch will handle only the build queue formed after that object enters `.github/workflows`, along with the version records for artifacts produced by the queue. The two paths will not take over each other's rollback actions: when one branch needs a rollback, handle it first using that branch's own artifact version, and do not also mark the other path's artifacts as unavailable.

This arrangement deliberately leaves caller migration out of scope. It has not yet been verified who currently calls `operation poller`; until that question is answered, the trial branch should not replace its existing call relationship. The project has its own schedule and maintainer, but whether the trial starts and who integrates it still need to be confirmed separately.

One objection is that splitting out `Web App` will leave two entry points in place, so troubleshooting will first require determining which side a request landed on. This cost is acceptable only if the build queue and artifact versions can retain separate records and different failure exits are no longer collapsed into a single result. If that cannot be done, keeping two entry points only adds another decision without producing clearer rollback boundaries.

Rollback will not delete the old path, nor does it promise to restore any callers that have not been confirmed. First stop the new branch from entering the queue, retain the version records for artifacts already generated, then restore the old entry point as the only processing path. If the call relationship for `operation poller` is clarified during this period, add it to the decision separately; do not substitute the assumption in this proposal for it.

Pending confirmation:

- The current callers of `operation poller`;
- whether the `Web App` branch can independently retain artifact version records;
- whether any trigger points besides the old entry point need to be restored during rollback.

This page covers a failed run of emulator-compatibility-catalog. The goal is not to fill in the catalog, but to preserve the original input and state at the first failure point so the next shift can continue from the same place.

- Have the original emulator-compatibility-catalog for this run on hand; don't create a similar input to replace it.

1. Replay from the original record in the catalog, recording only the steps actually taken.

After stopping, retain the original catalog entry, the output already observed, and any gaps in the record. If there is no original record, don't fill it in as a zero result; distinguish an observed zero result from data not collected. Recovery actions haven't been tried in the shared environment yet, so don't perform return or cleanup operations from this page.

This FAQ was originally treated as the sign-off rules for the shared entry point. It remains mainly because its first item once led people to mistake "can be imported" for confirmed behavior; later review did not support that inference.

If both sides provide only their own partial result, retain the candidate path and do not substitute "entry can be imported" for withdrawal confirmation. Retaining the entry point does not declare it problem-free, nor does it endorse any product behavior. It merely prevents a confounded observation from being expanded into an irreversible entry point decision. If the differences are later confirmed to come from product behavior, an entry point adjustment should not replace an assessment on the product side; if they come from cloud resource state, that state should be addressed first; if neither differs but the test environment remains unstable, the window's results still cannot be used as proof for an entry point choice.

The meeting required the actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that can be restored to be documented and retained. These three items cannot be filled in with speculation. What can currently be confirmed is that the differences under discussion hinder people's ability to determine whether the call chain from CLI to API is functioning normally; which usage scenarios are affected cannot yet be confirmed, much less described as a widespread failure of the existing entry point. In the next set of materials, actual impact should be demonstrated by call records under the same conditions, not inferred backward from results within a particular window.

The coordination arrangement is also limited to public entry point maintenance. The maintenance team is responsible for collecting recheck materials and bringing the relevant maintainers into the same review when different entry point arrangements need to be compared. The coordinator should deliver a record that can be reviewed afterward: the same Firebase project, the same region, the initiation point for CLI, and the corresponding API result. A verbal confirmation that "we tried it" cannot replace this record. This arrangement does not change the existing maintenance relationships for the product or cloud resources, nor does it transfer their assessments to the entry point maintenance team.

The recheck sequence is also fixed in this round. First fix the project and region, then initiate a call from CLI and trace it through to the response from API. If the project differs, the target resources may already differ; if the region differs, the resource state may also differ. Unless both conditions are fixed, the entry point choice is not the only change. Only when the call chain under the same conditions is retained can product behavior, target cloud resource state, and test environment noise be examined separately.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Current cli-routing entry point"] --> B["Reproduce in the same project and region"]
  B --> C["Corresponding record from CLI to API"]
  C --> D{"Where does the difference occur"}
  D --> E["Product behavior"]
  D --> F["Target cloud resource state"]
  D --> G["Test environment noise"]
  E --> H["Do not explain it in terms of the change window"]
  F --> H
  G --> H
  H --> I["Retain the old entry point and bring it back for review"]
```

The branches in the diagram are not an automated determination, nor do they call for rerunning every related command and resource. "Complete call" has a very narrow scope here: the record only needs to connect the CLI initiation point with the corresponding API result under the same conditions. If the record stops on the CLI side, it cannot distinguish whether the request failed to arrive, API returned a different result, or subsequent observations were affected by other conditions. If the record contains only the API result, it likewise cannot establish whether the entry point arrangement contributed to the difference.

The product behavior branch is explained by the API result. If API already shows a different product result under the same project and region, public entry point maintenance should not reframe that result as a window issue, much less conceal it by changing the entry point. The target cloud resource state branch requires separately documenting the resource state in the project and region being compared at the time; when resource states differ, the entry point comparison loses its meaning. Test environment noise needs to be retained as a separate phenomenon, rather than lumped under "environment issues" after reproduction fails. At a minimum, it must be possible to tell whether the noise appeared before CLI was initiated, after the API response, or during the observation steps between the two.

Someone proposed reversing the order: establish a change window first, see whether the results change, and then decide whether to continue retaining the old entry point. This approach was not adopted. Once the window goes first, incidental changes in the test environment, the resource state in a particular region, and product responses may all occur at the same time. Even if the results change, an explanatory gap remains: "Was it the window, the resources, or a product change?" The cost of retaining the current entry point is that subsequent decisions will take somewhat longer; the benefit is that the comparison still has a starting point that has not been quietly replaced.

The reversibility associated with the old entry point has two layers. First, until the change window is approved, the current entry point must remain in place and must not first be modified into a form that no longer allows comparison. Second, if a new entry point arrangement is approved later, it must still be possible to restore the arrangement retained in this round. No switching actions or restoration steps are defined in advance here; the specific handoff is handled separately by DOC-52. This decision constrains only the entry point choice: a new arrangement must not irreversibly replace the current baseline.

During a local lookup along the relationship from CLI to API, `src/ensureApiEnabled.ts` and its call name were examined. This location helps with discussing connection points near the entry point, but it cannot substitute for reproducing a run. The public entry point maintenance decision also does not depend on that file becoming the permanent home; the review focuses on whether the differences can be separated along the call chain, not on whether a particular filename looks like the sole entry point.

This round does not predefine a "successful result" for the change window. Specifying in advance that switching is allowed upon seeing a particular response would skip the assessment of whether product behavior and resource state are consistent. The materials brought back to the next review should first include three parts: records from CLI to API under the same conditions, the state of the target cloud resources when the differences were found, and an explanation of whether the test environment has independent noise. If any one of these parts is missing, the entry point arrangement still cannot be assessed as an independent variable.

Three assessments remain unresolved. Whether test environment noise alone is sufficient to cause the current differences has not been confirmed; how the change window would affect the call chain under the same project and region conditions has not been confirmed; no assessment of the scope of actual impact is yet available for reference. These are not incidental to-do items, but direct reasons for not approving a switch in this round. Describing them prematurely as "the entry point is unreliable" or "the window can fix it" would go beyond the available materials.

Therefore, only four decisions are currently in effect: maintain the cli-routing entry point; do not execute the change window; retain the old entry point for restoration and comparison; and have the public entry point maintenance team coordinate the next recheck from CLI to API under the same project and region. No decisions on product conclusions, resource conclusions, test environment attribution, or any switching time were made in this round.

## Assembly Order for the Next Round's Materials

To prevent the next review from again conflating the three types of differences into the single phrase "the entry point is unstable," assemble the materials in comparison order. The first page identifies only the baseline cli-routing entry point, Firebase project, and region, without assigning a cause in advance. The second page contains the CLI initiation point and the corresponding API result, preserving a verifiable link between them. The third page records the known state of the target cloud resources at the same moment; explicitly leave unknown fields blank rather than inferring them from the response. The fourth page lists test environment noise separately, including the observation step where it appeared and whether it invalidated this comparison.

This sequence is not a new approval process and does not change maintenance responsibilities. It merely allows the review to see which conditions were fixed and which remain unknown. The coordinator is responsible for bringing the materials to the same review and confirming that the comparison still uses the restorable old entry point as its baseline; the coordinator does not explain the results on behalf of product or resource maintainers. If the project, region, or entry point changes midway, these materials serve only as a record of one run and cannot support a switching decision.

Perform three checks first during the review. First, whether CLI and API come from the same project and region; if they cannot be matched, stop the entry point comparison. Second, whether the target resource state has been recorded separately; if not, leave the matter unresolved and do not attribute the differences to product behavior. Third, whether test environment noise is sufficient to invalidate the observations; if so, record where the noise occurred and repeat the call under the same conditions, rather than describing an incidental result as a benefit of the window. Only after all three checks can be answered should there be discussion of whether the change window warrants a separate, reversible comparison.

Continue to retain two columns on the final page of the materials: approved and not approved. The approved items remain limited to maintaining the current entry point, retaining the restoration baseline, and organizing a recheck under the same conditions; the unapproved items remain switching directly, using window results in place of causal attribution, and declaring the entry point failed without knowing the scope of impact. If new evidence emerges later, append the date and reasons beside these two columns rather than rewriting this round's decision, so that later readers can see how the conclusions changed.

## Boundaries of the Reversibility Conditions

In this record, "reversible" constrains only the entry point arrangement; it does not promise that product state or cloud resource state can be rolled back. Any future experiment must first save identifying information for the current entry point and specify in the review materials which baseline will be restored. If the baseline cannot be clearly identified, the change window does not enter execution discussions. This boundary also prevents a one-time improvement in the test environment from being mistakenly recorded as grounds for a permanent switch. The unresolved items remain for the next recheck under the same conditions.

# Shared Entry Point Switch Handoff Process

Handoffs for maintaining a shared entry point can become distorted at the last step: the person performing the switch sees that the task is finished, while the person taking over receives only a section of log and does not know which consumers have already left the old entry point. This lays out the handoff materials in switch order. The focus is not on adding a separate explanation for every secrets call, but on making the old entry point, candidate path, and rollback action line up in the same record.

The lookup for the entry point location is documented separately in DOC-53. This page only covers what should be left behind when consumers move from the old entry point to the candidate path, and when the status should still be written as migration in progress.

## Determining Whether the Handoff Is Complete

A switch must be able to answer at least three questions.

First, who the known consumers are and which ones are still using the old entry point. Here, "known" includes only consumers of secrets that have already been counted; callers that were not found cannot be considered migrated just because the trial run succeeded. Each row in the list should retain the consumer name, current entry point, path to be used, and whether it can roll back independently. When a consumer has no name, do not merge it into one row as "other callers."

Second, whether the candidate path has actually been used by a consumer that can roll back independently. This consumer is not a stand-in for full migration, but a small-scope switch record: it can return to the old entry point without waiting for another group to modify the shared entry point before it can recover. The rollback capability must be written down before the trial run; do not wait until the candidate path has a problem to guess whether the old entry point is still usable.

Third, whether the handoff package allows another person to reconstruct this operation. If any of the command parameters, request body, long-running task name, or terminal-state object is missing, it only shows that someone performed an action; it does not show that the person taking over can determine which step the action is at. The final log can serve as supporting evidence, but cannot replace the terminal-state object; logs often retain only the last sentence and do not preserve the old entry point, request content, or the object corresponding to the task.

If any one of these three questions is unanswered, the page status remains "migration in progress." This does not prevent a trial run; it avoids writing the partial result of the candidate path as if the shared entry point had already completed its switch.

## Retained from the Initial Draft: The Earlier Wrap-Up Approach

The initial draft made the process very short: count the consumers of secrets, choose one consumer that can roll back, run it through the candidate path, and hand off after success. This sequence still works, but the word "success" is too broad.

The earlier approach left at that time was:

```text
Old entry point -> Choose one consumer -> Candidate path -> Final log
```

This line did not identify the request body or explain how the long-running task name and terminal-state object belonged to the same trial run. More problematically, the earlier approach would lead the person taking over to treat the final log as the completion signal, with no place to record compatible callers that were still using the old entry point. This section is retained to show that the fields added later address a handoff gap rather than overturning the original trial-run sequence.

## Establish a Consumer Ledger First

Before starting the switch, the maintainer should create the following record for the known consumers. The fields do not need to be written as a project-level ledger; one trial run per row is sufficient. Leave cells without actual values blank; do not substitute example values.

| Consumer | Old entry point | Candidate path | Can roll back independently | Current record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Known consumer | Entry point used before the switch | Path used for this trial run | Where to return during rollback | Not started, in progress, or archived |

Write the actual entry point under "old entry point," not a generic term such as "default method." The candidate path should also be listed alongside the old entry point, so that someone does not later see only the new shared entry point name and fail to find the place that needs to be restored.

When counting consumers, first distinguish between two types of records. The first type is callers whose use of secrets has been confirmed; they enter this handoff ledger. The second type is compatible consumers that have been mentioned but whose use has not yet been confirmed; they must not be quietly included in the migrated count and should be listed separately after the ledger as uncovered callers. This makes it possible to state accurately after the trial run which type is covered, rather than giving a seemingly complete total.

Do not count the same consumer multiple times just because it has multiple logs. The handoff is concerned with whether it still depends on the old entry point and whether it has an independent rollback action. Multiple log fragments can only be attached to the record in the same row.

## Trial the Candidate Path

Before the trial run, select a consumer from the ledger that can roll back independently. The reason for the selection must be specific to this consumer: its old entry point is still usable, it can recover independently after the switch, and its operation record can be stored separately from those of other consumers. A consumer without a rollback action, Fang Ke, can remain in a later batch, but is not suitable as the first trial subject.

Complete the trial-run record in the order the events occur:

1. Write down the old entry point used by the consumer before the switch and the candidate path to be adopted.
2. Save the actual command parameters. The parameters must come from that operation; do not treat a command copied from elsewhere as the record for this operation.
3. Save the actual request body. Keep the request body and command parameters in the same trial-run record to avoid finding only half of them later.
4. Save the long-running task name. If the operation produces a long-running task, the name should correspond to this request; do not leave only a description saying "the task completed."
5. Save the terminal-state object. The terminal-state object is used to determine what state this candidate path ultimately produced; it is more suitable than the final log for judging the handoff.
6. Write down the rollback action and the old entry point after rollback. If the rollback action has not been recorded, do not mark this consumer as able to roll back independently.

If the candidate path does not produce an identifiable terminal-state object during the trial run, stop at that item; do not use the log to fill in the judgment. If the long-running task name is missing, return to the operation record and look for it instead of filling it in from memory. The fields in the handoff package must come from the same switch; combining the request body from one request with the task name from another will cause later readers to misjudge whether the problem is with the shared entry point or with the record itself.

After the trial run, the record should read as one continuous chain: which consumer left which old entry point, which candidate path it used, which parameters and request body it used, which long-running task it produced, and which terminal-state object it ended with; if recovery is needed, what should be done. This is more suitable for a handoff than attaching multiple screenshots, because screenshots usually cannot show whether they belong to the same operation.

## Expand from the Trial Run to the Remaining Consumers

After the candidate path has been trialed, do not immediately mark all known consumers as migrated. First mark the trial consumer separately in the ledger, and keep the others separated by old entry point and compatibility status.

Subsequent switches can be performed in small batches. Each batch should include only consumers already listed in the ledger, and should retain its own command parameters, request body, long-running task name, and terminal-state object. Do not share one "completed" conclusion between batches: the terminal-state object for one batch can only describe the consumers involved in that batch.

Compatible callers are the part most likely to be missed in a handoff. Even if they do not enter the candidate path for now, they should remain on the uncovered list, with the old entry point they still depend on documented. After the candidate-path records are complete, decide whether to include them in the next batch; until then, the old entry point remains a path that must be maintained.

Maintaining the old entry point does not mean continuing to add new consumers. During the switch, its purpose is to provide known callers with a recovery location and give the trial run's rollback action a real destination. If the maintainer removes the old entry point prematurely, subsequent rollback records lose their meaning, and the person taking over cannot distinguish a problem with the candidate path from a problem with the recovery path.

## How to Arrange the Handoff Package

Archive handoff materials by switch rather than scattering them by material type. The recommended reading order is:

```text
Consumer
  ├─ Old entry point before the switch
  ├─ Candidate path
  ├─ Command parameters
  ├─ Request body
  ├─ Long-running task name
  ├─ Terminal-state object
  └─ Rollback action and old entry point after recovery
```

The "terminal-state object" here is the primary record for judging the handoff; attach the final log only beside that object. If someone can provide only a log, leave the item in progress and hand it off only after the correspondence between the task and object can be restored.

When taking over, look at the consumer ledger first, then open each trial-run record. Do not work backward from a pile of tasks or logs to guess which consumers have been switched. The three statuses—migrated, in progress, and uncovered—should coexist in the ledger: they reflect facts about different consumers, not an unfinished document.

## Rollback and Retaining the Old Entry Point

The rollback action is responsible only for consumers that actually went through the trial run. When recording a rollback, it must be possible to see which old entry point it returns to from the candidate path, and whether the consumer remains in the ledger after returning to the old entry point. An operation without a separate recovery location should not be written as "can roll back independently."

If the candidate-path record is missing the request body, long-running task name, or terminal-state object, prioritize stopping the expansion of the migration scope. The old entry point that already exists can remain in place, and the missing fields can be marked under the corresponding consumer; do not delete the old path just to make the batch look complete.

When the old entry point can be taken offline depends on whether the known consumers and uncovered callers all have clear destinations. As long as the uncovered list still contains callers that depend on the old entry point, or any migrated record cannot be used to reconstruct its rollback action, the handoff should not describe the old entry point as removable.

## Addendum After This Review

The key addition from the review was not more logs, but downgrading the "final log" from the basis for completion to supporting material. The command parameters, request body, long-running task name, and terminal-state object that were not explicitly written in the initial draft are now parts that must be handed off with the record for every trial run.

Compatible callers that remain unconfirmed continue to be listed separately. They do not automatically acquire migration status just because the candidate path has been trialed. When the handoff for the shared entry point switch ends here, the person taking over should be able to continue maintaining the old entry point, recheck the candidate path, or perform the recorded rollback action for any one listed consumer.
